title: Design principles
scopeHtml: Scope: DRY, KISS, YAGNI, Law of Demeter, tell-don't-ask, composition over inheritance, separation of concerns, fail fast, least astonishment, immutability, and how they conflict. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why principles, not rules
notes.html:
Design principles are rules of thumb that predict which code will be cheap to change. They conflict sometimes (DRY pushes you to merge, YAGNI pushes you not to abstract yet), so a senior's skill is knowing which wins here and why. The cost being fought is always the same: the price of the next change.

Worked example. A feature touches 1 file in a well-designed module (1 hour) versus 9 files in a tangled one (1.5 days). Over 40 features a year that is 40 hours against 480 hours, a team-month, caused by design not typing speed.

Industry examples. Google's engineering practices doc favours readable, simple code over clever code. Basecamp and early Instagram stayed small on purpose (YAGNI at company scale).

Everyday analogy. Kitchen habits: label things (DRY), simple recipes (KISS), buy only what you will cook (YAGNI).

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting acronyms with no example of when a principle should be broken.
  • Treating principles as laws rather than trade-offs.

notes.title: DRY: one source of truth
notes.html:
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) means each piece of knowledge lives in exactly one place. It is about knowledge, not about identical-looking lines.

Before (the same rule in 3 places):

// OrderService
if (user.getAge() >= 18 && user.isVerified()) { ... }
// SignupController
if (age >= 18 && verified) { ... }
// ReportJob: someone changed it to > 18 (bug)
if (u.getAge() > 18 && u.isVerified()) { ... }

After:

final class Eligibility {
    static final int ADULT_AGE = 18;
    static boolean canPurchase(User u) { return u.age() >= ADULT_AGE && u.verified(); }
}
object Eligibility { const val ADULT_AGE = 18; fun canPurchase(u: User) = u.age >= ADULT_AGE && u.verified }

Worked example. The rule changes from 18 to 21 for a market: 1 edit versus finding 3 (and missing the one using >). A real incident pattern is two services computing "active subscription" differently, so billing charges users that the app shows as cancelled; the metric is a mismatch between billing count and active-user count.

Industry examples. OpenAPI schemas or protobuf files generate client and server code from one definition (single source of truth). Shopify and Stripe generate SDKs from API specs.

Everyday analogy. One master calendar everyone reads, instead of everyone keeping their own copy that drifts.

Decision gravity. Merging duplicates is reversible when they are internal. Sharing code between services via a common library couples their release cycles; that is close to a one-way door. Also, two things that look identical but change for different reasons are not duplicates: merging them (accidental duplication) creates a worse coupling than the copy. Wait for the rule of three.

Common interview traps.

  • Over-DRYing: a function with 8 boolean flags to serve 2 "similar" callers.
  • Forgetting DRY applies to config, schemas, docs and tests, not just code.

notes.title: KISS: keep it simple
notes.html:
KISS says choose the simplest design that meets the requirement. Simple means few moving parts and easy to explain, not "fewest lines".

Before (clever):

// 1 line, nobody can debug it
return Optional.ofNullable(u).map(User::cart).map(c -> c.items().stream()
    .filter(i -> i.qty() > 0).mapToLong(i -> i.price() * i.qty()).sum()).orElse(0L);

After (plain):

long total = 0;
if (u == null || u.cart() == null) return 0;
for (Item i : u.cart().items()) total += i.price() * i.qty();
return total;
fun total(u: User?): Long = u?.cart?.items?.sumOf { it.price * it.qty } ?: 0L

The Kotlin version is both short and clear; simplicity depends on the idiom of the language.

Worked example. A team added a message broker, 3 microservices and a saga for a feature serving 200 requests/day. A monolith with one transaction would handle 100x that on a single db.t3.medium. Operational cost: 3 deploy pipelines, on-call load, tracing. Simple would have shipped in 2 weeks instead of 3 months.

Industry examples. Stack Overflow served huge traffic with a small number of well-tuned servers. Basecamp ("majestic monolith"). Amazon Prime Video moved a monitoring service from distributed Lambda/Step Functions back to a single process and reported large cost savings (confirm figures in their engineering blog).

Everyday analogy. A hammer for a nail, not a robotic nailing arm.

Decision gravity. Choosing simple first is reversible: you can add complexity when a measured need appears. Premature complexity (distributed system, plug-in framework) is the expensive one-way door because you pay its cost every day.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing "simple" with "easy": a framework you already know is easy, but may not be simple.
  • Presenting a 12-box architecture for a CRUD app.

notes.title: YAGNI: you aren't gonna need it
notes.html:
YAGNI says do not build something because you might need it later. Speculative features cost time now, code to maintain, and are usually guessed wrong.

Before (speculative generality):

interface ExportStrategy { }
abstract class AbstractExporterFactoryProvider { }
class ExporterRegistry { /* plugin loader for formats, "in case we add PDF, XML, Parquet" */ }
// real requirement today: export CSV

After:

void exportCsv(List<Order> orders, Writer out) throws IOException {
    for (Order o : orders) out.write(o.id() + "," + o.total() + "\n");
}
fun exportCsv(orders: List<Order>, out: Appendable) = orders.forEach { out.append("${it.id},${it.total}\n") }

When the second format actually arrives, extract an interface then (a 20-minute refactor with tests).

Worked example. The plug-in framework: 3 days to build, 600 lines, 2 bugs, and 3 formats never added. Cost over two years including reading and maintaining: roughly 10 engineer-days for zero use. Industry studies (and the "Standish"-style numbers often quoted) suggest a large share of features are rarely used; treat such figures as folklore unless you can cite them, and measure your own usage with analytics.

Industry examples. Extreme Programming (Kent Beck, Ron Jeffries) coined it. Many startups ship a single-region, single-DB v1 and add sharding only at about 70% of measured capacity.

Everyday analogy. Not buying a canoe because you might move to a lake house.

Decision gravity. YAGNI is safe when the change is cheap later (adding a class, a column, an endpoint). It is wrong when the change is a one-way door that is cheap now and ruinous later: for example, adding an id and a created_at to every table, UTC timestamps, API versioning, idempotency keys on payments. Those are not speculation, they are known costs of retrofit.

Common interview traps.

  • Using YAGNI as an excuse to skip tests, security or migrations.
  • Not distinguishing "the requirement exists, just later" (plan for it) from "someone might want it" (do not build).

notes.title: Law of Demeter: talk to friends
notes.html:
The Law of Demeter (least knowledge) says an object should only call methods on itself, its fields, its parameters, and objects it created. Avoid a.getB().getC().doThing() train wrecks.

Before:

String city = order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity();     // knows 3 classes
double fee = order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry().getTaxRule().rate();

After:

class Order {
    String shippingCity() { return customer.shippingCity(); }
}
class Customer {
    String shippingCity() { return address.city(); }
}
String city = order.shippingCity();
class Order(private val customer: Customer) { fun shippingCity() = customer.shippingCity() }

Worked example. If Address.city is renamed to a Location object, the "before" version breaks in every one of 40 callers; the "after" version changes only Customer.shippingCity(). Count the dots in a line (more than 2 across different types) as a smell, but a fluent builder or stream chain on one type (list.stream().filter().map()) is fine.

Industry examples. Hibernate lazy-loading plus deep chains in views produces N+1 queries and LazyInitializationException. Android's context.getResources().getDisplayMetrics().density is a Demeter violation that tests struggle to fake.

Everyday analogy. You ask your friend to pass the salt; you do not reach into their pocket for their wallet.

Decision gravity. Adding delegating methods is cheap but can bloat classes with pass-through methods (middle man). It is a trade: fewer callers coupled to internals versus more surface. Reversible.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting dots mechanically; the real rule is about knowledge of structure, and data transfer objects with plain getters are exempt.
  • Fixing with dozens of one-line wrappers instead of moving the behaviour (see tell, don't ask).

notes.title: Tell, don't ask
notes.html:
Tell, don't ask means tell an object what to do instead of pulling its data out and deciding for it. Behaviour belongs next to the data it uses.

Before (ask, then decide outside):

if (account.getBalance() >= amount && account.getStatus() == Status.ACTIVE) {
    account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount);
} else {
    throw new IllegalStateException();
}

After (tell):

account.withdraw(amount);          // the account checks its own rules
account.withdraw(amount)
 Before: Caller reads balance, status, then writes balance   (logic duplicated in every caller)
 After:  Caller --withdraw()--> Account { rules + state }    (logic once)

Worked example. Check-then-act outside the object has a race: two threads read balance 1000, both withdraw 700. Moving the logic inside lets the object (or its database UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= 700) make it atomic. It also removes the same check copied across 12 callers, one of which forgot the status test.

Industry examples. Anemic domain models (Fowler's anti-pattern) in Spring apps put all logic in *Service classes with entities as data bags; rich domain models in DDD put behaviour on the entity. Actor systems (Akka, Erlang) enforce tell by design: you send messages, you cannot read internal state.

Everyday analogy. Tell the waiter "I'd like the pasta"; do not walk into the kitchen to check stock and cook it yourself.

Decision gravity. Moving logic into entities is reversible. Not every read is a violation: queries, reports and DTOs legitimately ask (CQRS separates the read side). Use judgement.

Common interview traps.

  • Dogmatic: "never use getters". Views and serialisation need them.
  • Treating it as the same as Demeter; they overlap but Demeter is about reach, this is about where logic lives.

notes.title: Composition over inheritance
notes.html:
Prefer building behaviour by combining small objects over extending a parent class. Has-a with delegation is more flexible than is-a.

Before (inheritance explosion):

class Bird { void fly() { } }
class Penguin extends Bird { void fly() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } }  // LSP violation
// add swimming, loud, trained... : FlyingSwimmingBird, FlyingLoudBird ...

After (compose abilities):

interface Movement { void move(); }
class Flying implements Movement { public void move() { /* flap */ } }
class Swimming implements Movement { public void move() { /* paddle */ } }

class Animal {
    private Movement movement;                       // swappable at runtime
    Animal(Movement m) { this.movement = m; }
    void setMovement(Movement m) { this.movement = m; }
    void go() { movement.move(); }
}
Animal penguin = new Animal(new Swimming());
interface Movement { fun move() }
class Animal(private var movement: Movement) { fun go() = movement.move() }
// Kotlin delegation removes the forwarding boilerplate:
class Duck(m: Movement) : Movement by m
 Inheritance: Bird <- FlyingBird <- LoudFlyingBird ...  (combinatorial)
 Composition: Animal --has--> Movement (Flying | Swimming) , Sound (Loud | Quiet)

Worked example. 3 movement types x 3 sound types = 9 subclasses by inheritance versus 3 + 3 = 6 small classes with composition, and no new class when you add a 4th sound (only 1). Changing behaviour at runtime (a bird swapping to Swimming) is impossible with inheritance, trivial with composition.

Industry examples. Android moved from deep Activity inheritance to ViewModel, LifecycleObserver and Jetpack Compose (functions composed together). The Strategy, Decorator and Composite patterns in the GoF book are all composition; the book itself states the principle. Go and Rust have no class inheritance at all.

Everyday analogy. Lego bricks you snap together versus a one-piece moulded toy.

Decision gravity. Starting with composition is cheap and reversible; starting with inheritance is a one-way door, since removing a base class means rewriting subclasses and every caller relying on the supertype. Inheritance remains right for a stable, true is-a with real code reuse (for example AbstractList).

Common interview traps.

  • "Never use inheritance": false, but justify each use.
  • Delegation boilerplate: Kotlin by, Lombok @Delegate, or IDE generation helps.
  • Fragile base class: a child that depends on how the parent calls its own methods.

notes.title: Separation of concerns and fail fast
notes.html:
Separation of concerns (SoC) means each part of the code deals with one concern. Layers are the typical example: controller handles HTTP, service handles business rules, repository handles storage. Fail fast means detect a problem at the earliest point and stop loudly, instead of passing bad data along.

Before (mixed concerns, late failure):

@PostMapping("/pay")
String pay(@RequestBody Map<String,Object> body) {
    String amt = (String) body.get("amount");                          // could be null
    Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(URL);                   // SQL inside controller
    c.createStatement().execute("UPDATE wallet SET bal = bal - " + amt);  // SQL injection, NPE later
    return "ok";
}

After:

record PayRequest(@NotNull @Positive Long cents, @NotBlank String walletId) { }

@PostMapping("/pay")
void pay(@Valid @RequestBody PayRequest r) { walletService.debit(r.walletId(), r.cents()); }   // HTTP concern

class WalletService {                                                                          // business concern
    void debit(String id, long cents) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(id);
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cents");
        repo.debit(id, cents);
    }
}
data class PayRequest(val cents: Long, val walletId: String) {
    init { require(cents > 0) { "cents must be positive" }; require(walletId.isNotBlank()) }
}

Worked example. A null amount accepted at the edge travels through 4 layers and explodes in a nightly report 8 hours later; debugging takes half a day. Rejected at the controller it returns HTTP 400 in 2 ms with a clear message. Also: fail fast at startup. A service with a missing config key should crash on boot (the orchestrator shows CrashLoopBackOff immediately) rather than start and fail on the first payment. Spring's @ConfigurationProperties validation and Kubernetes readiness probes support this.

Industry examples. Stripe validates request parameters and rejects with a precise 400 error naming the param. Clean/Hexagonal architecture (Robert Martin, Alistair Cockburn) formalises SoC. The Erlang/Elixir "let it crash" philosophy plus supervisors is fail fast with recovery.

Everyday analogy. An airport: check-in, security, boarding are separate stations, and a bad ticket is stopped at the first one, not at the aircraft door.

Decision gravity. Layer boundaries are cheap early; merging or re-slicing layers later is a big refactor. Over-layering (5 layers of pass-through calls for a CRUD app) violates KISS. Fail fast is almost always correct, but for a public API be careful: returning errors to external callers is a contract; do not change codes lightly.

Common interview traps.

  • Catching an exception and returning null or an empty list; it hides the failure (swallowed exception).
  • Confusing fail fast with crash the whole process on a recoverable error such as a single bad record in a batch (log, skip to dead-letter queue, alert).
  • Validating only at the UI; always validate at the server trust boundary.

notes.title: Least astonishment and immutability
notes.html:
Principle of least astonishment (POLA): a method should do what its name and signature suggest, and nothing surprising. Immutability: an object that never changes after creation is easier to reason about, safe to share between threads and safe as a map key.

Before (surprising and mutable):

List<Item> sorted = cart.getItems();        // getter that returns the internal list
Collections.sort(sorted);                    // sorts the cart's own data! surprise
class Money { public long cents; }          // anyone can change it, anywhere

After:

List<Item> items() { return List.copyOf(items); }       // defensive copy, read-only

final class Money {
    private final long cents;
    private final String currency;
    Money(long cents, String currency) { this.cents = cents; this.currency = Objects.requireNonNull(currency); }
    Money plus(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(cents + o.cents, currency);         // new object, original unchanged
    }
}
// Java 16+: record Money(long cents, String currency) { }
data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String) {
    operator fun plus(o: Money): Money { require(currency == o.currency); return copy(cents = cents + o.cents) }
}
 Mutable:   a ---> [Money 500]    b ---> same object ; b.add(100) also changes a   (surprise)
 Immutable: a ---> [Money 500]    b = a.plus(100) ---> [Money 600] new ; a unchanged

Worked example. A HashMap<Money, String> with a mutable key: put with cents=500, mutate to 600, then get returns null because the hash bucket is stale. With an immutable key this bug cannot exist. For concurrency, immutable objects need no locks: 16 threads reading a shared immutable config need zero synchronisation, while a mutable one needs a lock or a volatile snapshot. Cost: every change allocates a new object (a tiny cost for small objects; for large collections use persistent structures such as Kotlin's kotlinx.collections.immutable, Vavr, or Guava ImmutableList).

Industry examples. Java's String, Integer, LocalDate; Redux/Jetpack Compose state as immutable snapshots; Git commits (content-addressed, never edited); event sourcing stores immutable events (Kafka log, bank ledgers append-only). Collections.unmodifiableList is only a read-only view, not immutable, whereas List.copyOf is a true copy.

Everyday analogy. A printed receipt versus a whiteboard: the receipt cannot be quietly changed, so everyone can trust it.

Decision gravity. Starting immutable is cheap and reversible (add a builder or copy later). Starting mutable and later making things immutable breaks every caller that mutates: a one-way door. For value objects (money, dates, ids), choose immutable by default.

Common interview traps.

  • final field or variable does not make the referenced object immutable (final List can still be added to).
  • Immutable class rules: final class, final fields, no setters, defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs.
  • Surprising defaults: Date/Calendar are mutable, use java.time; method named get that hits the network.

notes.title: Principles in tension
notes.html:
Principles collide; the senior answer picks one and says why.

Conflict Resolution
DRY vs YAGNI/KISS Duplicate twice, abstract on the third; merge only when the knowledge is truly the same
DRY vs decoupling Copying a small helper into two services can beat a shared library that couples their releases
Tell-don't-ask vs SoC Keep rules in the domain, keep I/O (HTTP, DB) at the edge
Immutability vs performance Immutable by default; mutable inside a measured hot loop, hidden behind the class boundary
Fail fast vs availability Fail fast on programmer errors and bad config; degrade gracefully on runtime outages (retries, fallback)

Worked example (review comment). Two services both format phone numbers with 6 identical lines. Reviewer A says "extract a shared lib". Better: the rules may diverge per country soon, the lines are tiny, and a shared lib creates a version-lock; accept the duplication, and add a contract test if the format must match. This is the kind of reasoning that distinguishes senior answers.

Industry examples. Google's monorepo shares code liberally (with strong tooling); Amazon's two-pizza services prefer duplication to shared libraries (accept duplicated code to keep services independently deployable).

Everyday analogy. Diet advice: eat protein, avoid sugar, enjoy cake sometimes. Rules guide, judgement decides.

Common interview traps.

  • Defending a principle absolutely instead of naming the context and cost.
  • Not giving a concrete example from your own code when asked "when did you break DRY?".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• DRY: one source of truth for knowledge, not for lookalike code; wait for the third use; shared libraries couple releases.
  • KISS: the simplest design that meets measured needs; complexity is a daily running cost.
  • YAGNI: do not build speculative features, but do pay for cheap-now, ruinous-later basics (ids, UTC, versioning, idempotency).
  • Law of Demeter: talk to neighbours, not their internals; hide structure behind intent-revealing methods.
  • Tell, don't ask: put behaviour with the data; keeps rules in one place and makes atomicity possible.
  • Composition over inheritance: small swappable parts beat base-class hierarchies; inheritance only for true, stable is-a.
  • Separation of concerns and fail fast: layers with one job, validation at trust boundaries, crash on bad config at startup.
  • Least astonishment and immutability: predictable names and no leaked internals; immutable value objects are thread-safe and map-key safe.
  • Principles conflict; state the trade-off and whether the decision is reversible.
